# The Light Company

> Prism brings projected guidance and camera-based observation to physical work. The public website explains Prism Robotics and Prism IRL. The company has also used the name lght.co.

## Product and evidence

- [Prism Robotics](https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics): projected staging, camera-based scene checks and the workflow for connecting physical conditions to trials.
- [How it works](https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics/how-it-works): define, calibrate, stage, verify, run, review and revisit.
- [Technical brief](https://lightcompany.ai/media/prism-technical-brief.pdf): company-authored mechanism and limitations. Operational estimates are from limited partner context, not independent universal measurements.
- [Lab films](https://lightcompany.ai/gallery): recorded demonstrations, not proof of universal accuracy or compatibility.
- [Prism IRL](https://lightcompany.ai/prism): projected interfaces for everyday surfaces.

## Product walkthroughs and sample data

- [Scene history](https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics/scene-history): interactive walkthrough of scene history using example data. Prism keeps scene revisions connected to evaluation records; the public controls demonstrate the workflow in a diagram.
- [Benchmarks](https://lightcompany.ai/benchmarks): illustrative scores and sample trial records. Do not cite them as measured model performance, a winner or a vendor endorsement.

## Full editorial text

# Evaluate robot policies in the real world.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics

Prism stages the scene, verifies the setup and records every rollout. Compare models under the same conditions, find where they fail and replay the tests that matter.

## One workflow for physical evaluation.

Prism combines a station above the workcell with software for running and reviewing evaluations. The station uses projection to show the target setup and cameras to check the physical scene. The console connects that scene to the policy, recording and result. Your team can run a repeatable test suite, compare checkpoints and investigate failures without rebuilding the context of each trial by hand.

## Stage. Verify. Run. Review.

Stage the scene Choose a test condition. Prism projects object positions and placement guidance onto the work surface so an operator can prepare the scene. Verify the setup Check the camera observation against the target. Review placement differences and missing objects before accepting the rollout. Run the policy Execute the task with your robot and policy. Keep the condition, checkpoint and recording connected to the episode. Review the result Score each step against the task rubric. Inspect the evidence, flag abnormal runs and keep notes and corrections with the result. Repeat the test Return to a saved condition, stage it again and compare the next run. Use the same cases to check whether a new checkpoint improved. See the complete evaluation workflow .

## Git for your physical space.

Save a scene as a versioned condition. Change an object, its position or the surrounding setup. Keep the original, compare the revisions and return to either one for another evaluation. Scene history connects the intended setup, observed state and resulting episodes. When a result changes, your team can inspect both the policy version and the physical conditions behind it. Replay turns a saved condition back into staging guidance. The operator restores the objects and Prism checks the setup before the next run. Explore scene history .

## Find the conditions behind the score.

Change position, orientation, clutter, objects or lighting, then compare outcomes across the tested conditions. A capability map shows where the policy succeeds, where it fails and where you need more trials. Inspect task-level results, compare checkpoints and open the episodes behind a weak region. Keep trial counts and untested conditions visible so a strong average does not hide a recurring failure. The benchmark workspace brings rankings, model comparison, capability maps and trial records into one view. Its public dataset is a sample; the interface is ready to show your evaluation results.

## Use the workcell you already have.

A Prism station brings together projection, cameras and local compute above the workspace. It guides the person preparing the scene while the robot runs through its existing control system. Set up the station around the robot's reach, the objects and the camera view. Define the placement tolerances and task rules, then connect the evaluation workflow your team uses. Manage repeated conditions across operators and stations. Keep the scene definition, calibration reference and run context attached to the record so comparisons stay understandable as the lab grows.

## Run the lab from one workspace.

Define tasks and scoring rubrics, assign evaluations to operators and compatible stations, and manage the queue across the lab. Each task can include multiple object placements, step-level scoring conditions and a success threshold. Model presets keep the checkpoint, inference settings and relevant training context together. Evaluation definitions retain the task and model configuration so the comparison stays traceable.

## Bring your existing test library.

Import task and placement definitions from Notion or CSV, or connect an existing system through the connector API. Assign the resulting tests to stations and keep new imports in the library's history. Export results as CSV and save reports for the team. Compare models by task success, progress through the task and execution time, then open the runs behind the result.

## Every result has a record.

Open a run to inspect its camera recording, 3D telemetry, placement and step-by-step scores. Keep notes and attachments with the episode. Review flagged runs separately and retain the reason a trial was replaced. Use those records to investigate a failure, reproduce a regression or share a comparison with another researcher. The next person should be able to understand the experiment without asking who set up the table. Read the evaluation guides or download the technical brief .

## Common questions

Is Prism a simulator? Prism Robotics runs around physical robot workcells. It controls and checks the setup for real-world evaluations, then connects conditions and results in the console. Who resets the objects? An operator follows the projected placement guidance. Prism checks the scene against the target before the trial is accepted. The robot continues to use its own control system. How are rollouts scored? Your team defines scoring conditions for each task step and the threshold for success. Reviewers score the run against that rubric, flag abnormal trials and keep the decision with its supporting evidence. How do we get started? Book a demo with your robot, task and current evaluation process. We will work through station placement, integrations and the first test suite. You can also register interest in a station .

# From scene setup to a comparable result.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics/how-it-works

Prism connects the physical setup to the evaluation record. Each run starts from a defined condition and ends with an outcome your team can inspect.

## Define the task and test conditions.

Choose the task, objects, policy checkpoint and success criteria. Specify the timeout, allowed interventions and reasons to reject a rollout. Save the protocol so every candidate is evaluated against the same rules. Build a test suite from the conditions you want to cover. Start with a baseline, then add the changes that matter for your use case.

## Set up the station around your workcell.

Register the camera and projector to the work surface. Check the field of view, mounting and placement accuracy against the objects and robot reach. Prism keeps the calibration reference with the scene context. When equipment moves or the workspace changes, check the station before reusing existing conditions.

## Project the target scene.

Select a saved condition or create a new one. Prism projects placement targets and labels directly onto the table. The operator positions the objects using the guidance in the workspace. Change the condition without redrawing marks or rebuilding a fixture. The scene definition stays available for the next operator and the next run.

## Verify before the rollout starts.

Cameras compare the prepared scene with the intended condition. Review missing objects, placement differences and the task's acceptance criteria before running the policy. The record keeps the target and observation distinct. A setup rejection is handled separately from a valid trial that the policy fails.

## Run the policy and capture the episode.

Your robot executes the task through its existing control system. Prism connects the episode to the scene, policy version and evaluation protocol. Keep the recording and any intervention with the run. Use a consistent protocol for when projected guidance is visible so it does not become an unintended cue during policy evaluation.

## Score, inspect and compare.

Score each task step against the evaluation rubric. Review camera recordings and telemetry, flag abnormal runs and record the reason for a correction. Keep the score, reviewer and timestamps with the result. Compare candidates on the same test suite. Move from an aggregate score to task results, individual trials and the conditions behind a failure.

## Replay a failure against the next checkpoint.

Select a saved condition and project the setup again. Restore the objects, verify the scene and run the new policy. Compare the episodes using the same task definition. Build regression suites from the cases your team wants to retain. Scene history keeps those cases connected as the setup and policy evolve.

# Version your scenes. Replay your evaluations.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics/scene-history
Status: interactive product walkthrough with example data.

Keep a versioned record of the physical setup. Change one condition, compare the result and return to the same test when a new checkpoint is ready.

## Keep the scene with the run.

A scene record connects the objects, target arrangement and station configuration to the task. Every episode can refer back to the condition it started from. Review the intended setup alongside the observed state. Keep the policy version, recording and result attached so the experiment remains useful after the session ends.

## Change one condition at a time.

Create a revision from a baseline scene. Move the target, turn it, introduce clutter, substitute an object or change the lighting setup. Preserve the original condition and name the difference. Use those revisions to build a test suite that answers a specific question. Compare matched conditions across policies, then examine combinations when you want to test interactions.

## See what changed and what happened.

Compare scene versions together with their episodes. Inspect the setup difference, policy checkpoint and outcome, then open the evidence behind the score. A change in the rubric or station configuration belongs in that comparison too. The record gives the team a common reference when a result improves or regresses.

## Restore the setup for another run.

Select a saved condition and re-project its placement guidance. The operator restores the objects, the station checks the scene, and the new episode joins the same evaluation history. Use replay to investigate a failure, test a fix or compare a checkpoint against the cases your team wants to retain.

## Build a regression suite from real failures.

Keep important scenes in a shared test library. Assign them to stations, organize runs and review results with the people responsible for the task. A failure should become a reusable test case. Scene history makes it possible to find the setup, understand the previous result and run the question again. See scene history in a demo or read the guide .

# The company behind Prism.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/company

We build evaluation tools for physical AI. Prism combines projection, perception and software so robotics teams can run repeatable tests and understand their results.

## Make robot evaluations more useful.

Robotics teams need to know whether a new policy is better, where it fails and whether a result can be reproduced. That requires control over the physical setup and a clear record of what happened. We build the station and software that connect those parts of the workflow. Operators can prepare a defined scene, researchers can compare matched conditions, and the team can review the evidence behind a result.

## Our products

Prism Robotics The evaluation platform for physical AI. Stage and verify scenes, run test suites, score rollouts, compare policies and retain the conditions behind each result. Explore Prism Robotics . Prism IRL Projected interfaces for everyday surfaces. Prism combines vision and light to put information and guidance where people are working. Explore Prism IRL .

## Built across hardware, software and robotics.

Our team brings experience from Apple engineering and Carnegie Mellon research. We work across station hardware, perception, evaluation software and the operator experience. The product is developed around real workcells and the people running them. A useful evaluation tool needs to fit the reset process, preserve the right evidence and make the next decision easier.

# How to plan a real-world robot evaluation
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/resources/robot-evaluation

Define the task, control the starting conditions and agree on scoring before you run the evaluation.

## Define the evaluation question

Are you choosing between two checkpoints, testing whether a new object breaks a skill, or deciding whether a workflow is ready for a specific setting? These are different decisions. They deserve different experiments. Write the decision in one sentence. Then describe the evidence that would change your mind. Use that decision to set the test scope and required evidence. A practical example: “We want to know whether the new checkpoint improves placing this mug in this tray across the positions used at this workcell.” That question names the policy change, task, objects and scope. It leaves room to report what was not tested.

## Set the scoring rules

Define success in observable terms. Specify the time limit, allowed contact, acceptable final state and any permitted assistance. Decide how to handle interruptions, sensor loss, a bad reset or a stopped robot. Keep three outcomes separate: a valid success, a valid failure and an invalid or unresolved episode. A reset mistake should not silently count against the policy, and removing a difficult valid failure would make the report misleading. When two reviewers disagree, retain the disagreement and resolve it against the rubric. A scoring model can help organize review, but its answer still depends on the evidence and instructions it receives.

## Choose the test conditions

List the conditions that matter: object identity, position, orientation, clutter, lighting, camera arrangement, robot start state and relevant surface properties. Choose which to hold fixed and which to vary deliberately. Begin with a baseline that can be described and restored. Then choose a schedule of conditions that answers the question. Repeating an easy scene many times does not establish performance across a wider set of scenes. Give every intended condition an identifier. Record what was actually staged and whether it met the acceptance rule. A projected target is useful, but the target is not proof that the object arrived there.

## Record each trial

At minimum, connect each episode to the task and rubric versions, policy or checkpoint identity, scene condition, robot configuration, outcome and any intervention. Where recordings are collected, preserve their relationship to the episode and handle access according to the team's data agreement. Here is a downloadable evaluation checklist . It is a planning aid, not a Prism API contract. What was the intended setup, and how was it checked? Which policy ran, with which robot and sensor configuration? Was projected guidance visible during the recording? What happened, and what evidence supports the score? Did anyone intervene, discard a trial or change a rule? Which conditions remain untested?

## Report the results and test scope

Give the number of trials and successes, the conditions covered, the uncertainty appropriate to the experiment and the reasons for exclusions. Explain the important failure modes in words. A single average can hide the condition that matters most to the team using the robot. Compare policies on a matched set of conditions where possible. Consider trial order and wear: running one candidate first all day and another after the objects or hardware have changed can introduce another difference. The Robot Learning as an Empirical Science: Best Practices for Policy Evaluation paper calls for more informative reporting than a bare success rate. This guide applies that principle to a workcell planning conversation; it does not prescribe a universally sufficient trial count. Next: why initial conditions belong in the result .

# Why robot evaluation starts with the reset
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/resources/initial-conditions

Consistent starting conditions make policy comparisons easier to interpret. Record the intended setup, check the scene and track changes between trials.

## How setup changes affect results

A mug returns to the table, almost where it was. The handle turns a little. A cable lies closer to the gripper. Nothing about the model changed, but its next observation did. That does not make variation a mistake. A capable robot must operate through variation. The problem is variation that enters the evaluation without being chosen, measured or described. When a team compares two policies, it needs to understand whether the policies faced comparable conditions. Otherwise a changed result may reflect a changed scene, a changed policy or both.

## Define, observe and verify the setup

Intended condition The scene the protocol asks for: objects, target positions and other declared conditions. Observed condition What the camera or operator can actually establish about the prepared scene. Acceptance decision Whether the observed scene is suitable for this trial under the task's tolerances, including any unresolved uncertainty. Collapsing these into one “ready” flag makes the interface simple at the expense of the experiment. A useful system lets a reviewer recover the reason the trial was accepted.

## Use projected setup guides

Prism projects placement guidance onto the work surface so an operator can prepare a target condition without referring back and forth to a separate drawing. Camera registration connects the projected instruction to the observed workspace. The Prism technical brief describes this as an initial-condition layer: stage, verify, log and re-project a saved condition. It also identifies limits. Planar placement is easier to express than a complete three-dimensional configuration; deformable objects and lighting need additional treatment. Visible projected marks may themselves affect a vision policy. The recording protocol must specify when guidance is shown and when it is removed. “No tape on the table” is helpful only if the replacement does not introduce an unexamined cue.

## Repeat the reset consistently

Start by naming the objects and the target arrangement. Check calibration against the actual workspace. Stage the scene, inspect the observation and record the acceptance decision. Only then begin the policy episode. When a reset cannot meet the requirement, preserve that fact. Do not quietly substitute a nearby scene while retaining the original condition label. When the table, camera or projector moves, re-check the relationship before using old targets. This is not a claim that every source of variability can be eliminated. It is a way to make the setup part of the experiment instead of an invisible assumption.

## Track each variable

Once a baseline is understood, move beyond it deliberately. Change one axis and record it. Then test combinations where interactions matter. The resulting capability map can show where a policy's performance changes across the conditions tested. For background on richer physical evaluation reporting, see Robot Learning as an Empirical Science: Best Practices for Policy Evaluation . For the product workflow, see how Prism works .

# Capability maps for robot evaluation
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/resources/capability-maps

Break down policy performance by position, orientation, clutter, objects and lighting. See which conditions cause failures and where more trials are needed.

## Look beyond aggregate success

Imagine two policies with similar overall results. One works across the table but struggles with a particular object. The other handles that object well but fails near the edge of the workspace. A single number can make them look interchangeable. A capability map organizes outcomes by the condition that produced them. It lets a team ask a practical question: does this policy work in the part of the world we actually care about? The map is an account of tested conditions. It does not establish capability in every untested scene, and it is not a safety certification.

## Five variables to test

Position What happens when the target moves across the reachable surface? Keep the camera and robot configuration recorded. Orientation What happens when the object turns? State which orientation is being varied and what can actually be verified. Clutter What happens when another object enters the scene? Record its identity and placement rather than calling everything “cluttered.” Objects What happens when the target changes? Size, material, shape and familiarity may change together; a substitution is rarely one perfectly isolated property. Lighting What happens when illumination changes? Record the lighting arrangement and relevant camera settings. Projected staging does not automatically control ambient light.

## Test individual variables and combinations

Begin with one axis at a time. It makes a failure easier to attribute and gives the team a readable first map. If the cup moves while the camera and light also change, the result cannot isolate the effect of position. After the first pass, test combinations that matter. Clutter and orientation may interact. A policy that tolerates either change alone may fail when both occur. One-variable tests are a useful beginning, not a complete account of the world. Colosseum is a simulation research example of evaluating environmental perturbations systematically. Its findings are not Prism measurements; the useful lesson here is to make the axes of variation explicit.

## Distinguish untested conditions

Show trial counts alongside outcomes. Mark untested conditions clearly. Preserve invalid episodes and review disagreements separately. If one cell contains many trials and another contains only a few, the visual treatment should not suggest equal certainty. Keep the task, rubric, policy and condition versions attached to the map. Comparing maps made under different rules can create a persuasive picture of a change that was never actually measured. Our benchmark workspace uses illustrative data to explore this interface. The public scores are sample data.

## Choose the next experiment

A useful map changes what the team does. It might reveal a narrow position boundary, motivate a new object test or identify a scene worth replaying against the next checkpoint. Preserve the conditions that led to that decision. Prism's role begins with making physical placement more explicit through projected guidance and camera checks. Scene history connects those conditions to the run record and the resulting comparison. Read about physical version control or bring us a task to discuss .

# Scene history for robot evaluation
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/resources/physical-version-control

Scene history keeps the test setup, model version and run evidence connected across evaluations.

## Why scene records matter

The video still exists. The result is in the spreadsheet. But the person who set up the table remembers the detail that makes it meaningful: a camera was moved, an object was substituted, a trial was restarted after an interruption. When that memory disappears, the record becomes harder to use. A new researcher can watch what happened without knowing enough to ask the same question again. Prism applies version history to the physical setup. Save a condition, create a revision and keep the resulting episodes connected to both the scene and policy version.

## Define the scene record

A scene record should connect the intended arrangement with what was observed: object identities, positions, calibration reference and the conditions the task depends on. A trial should point back to that record, not merely to a folder with a familiar name. A revision then describes a change. The cup moved. The object changed. The lighting arrangement was different. The old condition remains understandable, and the new one explains its relationship to it. That relationship is the beginning of a useful comparison. It also makes missing information visible: a field can be unknown rather than silently assumed to match.

## Compare scene revisions

In a physical experiment, a difference is not just something to display. It is often the reason to run the trial. Did the new policy improve on the old failure? Did changing the object reveal a dependency the team had not noticed? A useful history would keep the scene change, policy change and rubric change distinct. It would let someone review the evidence for the outcome and understand why a score was revised. The scene-history walkthrough shows how revisions work using an example scene.

## Recreate and verify the setup

Software can restore bytes exactly. A workcell cannot promise the same thing about friction, wear, exposure or the fold of a cloth. Projected guidance can help restore an arrangement; observation must still establish what was achieved. This is where the metaphor earns its limits. A scene history should not pretend to freeze the world. It should make the assumptions and tolerances of a reconstruction available for inspection. The Prism technical brief describes re-projecting a logged condition as a route to physical regression testing. Whether a specific task can be repeated closely enough remains something to measure in that task's setup.

## Share an evaluation your team can inspect

The destination is not a prettier archive. It is a lab where a failure remains findable, a comparison remains explainable and an old experiment can teach someone new. That asks for more than storage. It asks for names people understand, reasons kept beside decisions, permissions appropriate to the data and a way to say “we do not know” without breaking the workflow. Explore Prism Robotics , or tell us what your team's physical record is missing .

We aim to keep the website useful and accurate, but content may change and errors may occur. To the extent permitted by applicable law, the public website is provided as available without warranties about uninterrupted access, completeness or fitness for a particular purpose. To the extent permitted by law, we are not responsible for indirect or consequential losses arising from use of the public website. Nothing in these terms excludes rights, remedies or liabilities that cannot lawfully be excluded, including applicable consumer protections. No product warranty or service-level commitment is created by this website.

## Changes and contact

We may update these terms as the website changes. The date above identifies the current version. Material changes affecting a separate agreement will be handled according to that agreement and applicable law. For questions or to report inaccurate content, contact hi@lightcompany.ai with the page URL and a description of the concern.

# Privacy policy
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/privacy

This notice explains the information involved when you visit this website, register interest in Prism or contact us.

## Information you choose to provide

The station interest form asks for your name, email address and company or lab. Optional fields include your role, use case, robot or platform, estimated quantity and whether you want product updates. The service also records the source of the form, submission timestamps and the consent version. If you email us, we receive the information and attachments you choose to send, along with normal email metadata. This may include a product inquiry, support question, careers introduction or privacy request. Please avoid sending sensitive personal information, secrets, private credentials or other people's information unless an appropriate process has been agreed.

## Information involved in running the site

Website hosting, security and delivery providers may process technical information such as IP addresses, browser and device details, requested pages, timestamps and diagnostic information to deliver the website and protect their services. The site's benchmark introduction uses browser session storage to remember whether it has been dismissed. The scene-history walkthrough uses an example diagram and does not collect camera images. Some pages use third-party media, including YouTube. Loading or interacting with that content can send information to its provider. See cookies and storage for the current website features involved.

## Why we use information

We use inquiry information to answer you, discuss a possible deployment or collaboration, manage expressions of interest, provide requested support and maintain a record of those conversations. If you choose product updates, we may use your contact information for those updates; you can ask us to stop. Technical information helps deliver and protect the website, investigate problems and prevent abuse. We do not need personal details about your private life to discuss a workcell.

## Service providers and disclosures

Our public website is hosted through Sites infrastructure using Cloudflare services. Station-interest submissions are stored in the site's database. Email communications are handled through the email services used by the people communicating. Providers may process information to operate their services under their own applicable arrangements. We may also disclose information where necessary to comply with law, respond to a valid legal request, protect rights or address misuse. A separate product deployment may involve different providers or data flows; those should be agreed for that deployment. We do not sell the personal information submitted through this website. The website code does not include an advertising-pixel program. This notice does not describe third-party websites you visit through external links.

## Keeping and protecting information

We retain information for the purpose it was provided, including managing an ongoing conversation, meeting legal obligations and resolving disputes. Retention depends on the information and the context; this website does not promise a single fixed retention period for every system or backup. We use reasonable measures appropriate to the services we operate, but no online service can guarantee absolute security. Please contact us if you believe information has been sent to the wrong place or exposed unexpectedly.

## Your choices and requests

You can avoid optional form fields, decline product updates, clear browser storage and choose whether to follow external links. You may contact hi@lightcompany.ai to request access, correction or deletion of information you provided, or to stop product updates. Depending on where you live and the circumstances, applicable privacy law may give you additional rights. We may need to verify a request in a proportionate way and may retain information where required or permitted by law. Do not send identity documents in an initial request. This public website is intended for people exploring our work and business offerings; it is not directed to children. If you believe a child has provided personal information, contact us so we can investigate.

## Website data and lab data are different

This notice covers the public website and related inquiries. It does not establish the data arrangements for camera feeds, robot recordings, customer datasets or station deployments. Before a deployment, the parties should agree what is collected, where it goes, who can access it and how long it is kept. For privacy questions, contact hi@lightcompany.ai . We will update this notice when the public website's practices change.

# Cookies and storage
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/cookies

A small amount of browser state supports the website. Embedded services may have their own behavior.

## Storage used by the website

The benchmark introduction stores a dismissal flag in session storage under prism-benchmark-intro-v1 . It helps avoid repeatedly showing the same introduction during a browsing session. It does not contain your name or email. The public scene-history walkthrough keeps its selected example in the page while it is open. Reloading returns the walkthrough to its starting state. Hosting and security services may use cookies or similar mechanisms for delivery, abuse prevention or access controls. Their behavior can differ from the page's own scripts.

## Third-party content

The gallery uses YouTube's player technology. Loading that page or interacting with its player can contact YouTube and involve information such as your IP address and browser details. Third-party cookies and other processing are governed by the provider's settings and policies. Some older pages may request remotely hosted fonts. New company pages use locally hosted fonts. Following an external link takes you to a service with its own privacy practices.

## Your choices

You can remove cookies and site storage through your browser settings, block third-party cookies and choose not to load pages containing external media. Clearing storage may make an introduction appear again. The current website code does not include advertising pixels or a marketing analytics tracker. If additional non-essential tracking is introduced, its purpose and any required choices should be provided before it is used. For questions about personal information, see the privacy notice or contact hi@lightcompany.ai .

# Security and data
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/trust

Information about website data, deployment requirements and reporting a security concern.

## The public website

The website explains our work, hosts films and educational content, and collects station-interest submissions. It is separate from a customer's operational workcell. The public scene-history walkthrough is an interactive example, separate from a connected workcell. The station-interest endpoint validates submitted fields, limits request size, checks the request origin and stores accepted submissions in a database. Those are specific implementation measures, not a claim of comprehensive security certification. Read the privacy notice and browser-storage information for the public site's data practices.

## Before a station enters your lab

A deployment discussion should establish the data and operating boundaries before access is provided. Confirm the following requirements with your team: Which camera images, scene records and trial recordings are collected? What stays on the station, what is transmitted and where is it stored? Who can access the records, and how is access removed? How are updates, credentials, backups and incident contacts handled? What retention, export and deletion arrangements apply? Which actions require operator review, and which system controls the robot? Any customer-specific security commitments, data-processing terms, service levels or network requirements belong in the applicable written agreement.

## Claims you can inspect

Product pages explain Prism workflows and include recorded demonstrations. Sample data and operational estimates are labeled where they appear. The public benchmark scores are illustrative. This site does not assert SOC 2, ISO 27001 or another certification, nor does it promise universal compatibility or a guaranteed accuracy level. For the physical method and known constraints, read the technical brief . For a proposed deployment, ask us for evidence relevant to your actual task.

## Report a security concern

Email hi@lightcompany.ai with “Security report” in the subject. Include the affected URL or component, a clear description and non-sensitive reproduction steps. Do not include credentials, private customer data or harmful payloads in the initial message. Avoid accessing data that is not yours or disrupting a live service. This page is a reporting contact, not authorization to test private systems or a promise of a bounty.

# Accessibility
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/accessibility

Information about keyboard access, text, motion, media and assistance on this website.

## How we approach the website

The company pages use semantic headings, visible keyboard focus, a skip link, readable contrast and responsive layouts. Interactive controls have text labels. Motion respects the browser's reduced-motion preference where supported by the page. The scene-history walkthrough includes a text description of each change alongside its diagram. The ASCII footer is decorative and is hidden from assistive technology. We use the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a reference for improvement. This statement is not a claim of complete conformance or an independent accessibility audit.

## Known limitations

Some recorded demonstrations communicate information visually, and not every video has a complete caption or audio-description track. Some older pages and third-party players may have different accessibility behavior from the new company pages. If a film, document or interactive view prevents you from getting the information you need, tell us which content matters. We can discuss a text explanation or another way to share it.

## Report an accessibility issue

Email hi@lightcompany.ai with the page URL, what you were trying to do and what happened. If useful, include your browser or assistive technology, but do not send sensitive personal information. We welcome specific reports about keyboard access, contrast, text size, motion, media alternatives or confusing controls. A useful website should remain useful when someone's way of using it differs from ours.
